title: Structure: board, project manager, product owners and teams
blurb: Explain how the organization practice structures an agile project, from governance to self-managing delivery teams, with one team or many.
question: A project grows from one delivery team to three. How many project managers and product owners should it have, and who sets priorities across the teams?

teach.h: What the organization practice is for
teach.body: The organization practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities: in short, the 'who'. In PRINCE2 Agile it keeps the PRINCE2 governance roles and adds agile roles, so that self-managing delivery teams work inside clear boundaries. The principle behind it is 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships': the right people, clear roles and engaged stakeholders.

levels.label: Management
levels.sub: project manager, supported by project support

levels.label: Delivery team
levels.sub: product owner, team coach, developers, testers

teach.caption: Project assurance and the agile coach advise across levels. Based on Figure 7.1.

teach.body: The structure has two key links. The project manager is the only role with a direct line of authority over the product owner. The product owner, a version of the team manager role, is the only role with a direct line of authority over the delivery team members. The project manager agrees the team's work with the product owner as work package descriptions, which in agile are sets of user stories.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Figure 7.1, Table 7.2

teach.h: How work travels down the structure

steps.label: Project manager
steps.sub: runs the project day to day

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile asks leaders to serve. The project manager acts as a servant leader, linking governance and the teams; the product owner does the same at team level. Delivery teams self-manage how they do the work, within the tolerances their product owner has agreed with the project manager. That is why manage by exception sits at the heart of empowering people to self-manage while the project stays in control.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table 5.1

teach.body: Calderbrook Water is building a smart-meter app. Project manager Imogen Faulkner started with one team; the board now wants faster delivery, so two more teams join. Imogen stays the single project manager. Each team gets its own product owner, one team coach supports two of the teams, and chief product owner Rashid Okafor keeps the project backlog and sets priorities across all three. Imogen agrees sets of user stories with each product owner.

teach.text: Adding teams does NOT add project managers or merge the coaches. There is one project manager, possibly several product owners, a CPO prioritizing across teams, and the agile coach and team coach stay separate roles. The PM directs the PO, not the developers.

items: Organization practice: the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities (the 'who').
PM has the only direct line of authority over the PO.
PO, a version of the team manager, has the only direct line of authority over team members.
PM and PO agree work as work package descriptions, which are sets of user stories.
Many teams: one PM, possibly several POs, one CPO prioritizing across teams.
Team coaches work with one or two teams; teams keep the same make-up.

summary: You can now describe the agile project structure, including the two direct lines of authority and how work flows as sets of user stories. You can also say what changes, and what does not, when one team becomes several.

A.q: What is the purpose of the organization practice?
options: To control changes to the project's baseline
To compare actual progress against plans
To identify, assess and control uncertainty
To establish the structure of accountability
A.why: The organization practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities, the 'who' (7.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice.
whyNot.1: Comparing actual achievements with plans is the progress practice.
whyNot.2: Handling uncertainty is the purpose of the risk practice.

A.q: Which role has a direct line of authority over the product owner?
A.why: The project manager is the only role with a direct line of authority over the product owner (Figure 7.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: The CPO works closely with product owners and prioritizes across teams, but the reporting line runs to the PM.
whyNot.2: The team coach supports and advises the PO and team members; it has no authority over them.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administrative support and advice; it does not direct the PO.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what form does a work package description take when the project manager agrees work with a product owner?
options: An extract of the project backlog
A.why: The PM agrees the team's work with the PO as work package descriptions, which in agile are sets of user stories (Table 7.2, Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: The team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts the work package.
whyNot.1: The release map is the project or stage plan, not a work package.
whyNot.3: The project backlog holds the epics for the whole project and is owned by the CPO.

B.q: A project expands from one delivery team to four. Which change to the structure is expected?
options: A project manager is appointed for each team
There may now be a product owner for each team
The team coach and agile coach are merged into one role
Each team adopts a different set of delivery roles
B.why: With multiple teams there is one project manager and there can be more than one product owner (Figure 7.2).

whyNot.0: There is one project manager however many teams there are.
whyNot.2: The team coach and agile coach remain separate roles with different scopes.
whyNot.3: Multiple teams have the same composition as a single-team project.

B.q: Which role has a direct line of authority over the developers and testers in a delivery team?
B.why: The product owner, a version of the team manager role, is the only role with a direct line of authority over delivery team members (Figure 7.1).

whyNot.0: The team coach helps the team self-manage and improve; it does not hold authority over members.
whyNot.1: The project manager directs the product owner, not the individual team members.
whyNot.2: The project executive is accountable for the project at governance level.

B.q:
Which two statements about the agile project structure are correct?
1. The project manager acts as a servant leader linking governance and teams.
2. Each delivery team reports directly to the project board.
3. Product owners deliver within tolerances agreed with the project manager.
4. The chief product owner manages the day-to-day running of the project.
B.why: The PM is a servant leader linking governance and teams (1), and POs deliver within the tolerances and constraints agreed with the PM (3) (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: teams work through the PO and the PM, not directly to the board.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: teams do not report directly to the board, and day-to-day running belongs to the PM.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the CPO represents users and prioritizes across teams; the PM runs the project day to day.

C.q: On a three-team project, who sets priorities across the teams, and who owns each team's product backlog?
C.why: The CPO makes sure priorities are clearly defined across teams, and each PO owns their team's product backlog (Table 7.2, Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The PM does not prioritize across teams, and project support gives administrative help rather than owning a backlog.
whyNot.1: The executive is accountable at governance level; developers build products rather than own the backlog.
whyNot.3: The agile coach removes organization-level blockers; the PM does not own team backlogs.

C.q: Which principle does the organization practice MAINLY support, and what does PRINCE2 Agile add to it?
options: Manage by stages; timeboxed iterations and releases
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships; agile roles
Focus on products; user stories and acceptance criteria
Learn from experience; retrospectives and feedback loops
C.why: The organization practice puts 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' into effect; in agile, additional agile roles may be needed and PRINCE2 roles tailored carefully (5.2.1.3, Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage control; stages contain iterations and releases.
whyNot.2: Focus on products concerns defining outputs; user stories support plans and quality.
whyNot.3: Learn from experience is supported by retrospectives and feedback loops.

C.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile say manage by exception is at the heart of empowering teams?
options: Teams self-manage within tolerances while governance stays in control
Teams escalate every decision so the board can stay informed
Teams set their own time and cost tolerances for each iteration
Teams report to the board in place of the project manager
C.why: Delegating authority within tolerances lets teams self-manage while the project remains under control (Table 5.1).

whyNot.1: Escalating every decision is the opposite of empowerment; escalation is for forecast breaches of tolerance.
whyNot.2: Tolerances are set from above; time and cost have zero tolerance by default.
whyNot.3: Teams work through the PO and PM; they do not replace the PM's reporting line.

reteach.title: A relay, not a crowd
reteach.question: Picture a relay race. Who hands the baton to whom, and what happens when more runners join?

blocks.body: The board hands authority to the project manager. The project manager hands work to each product owner as a set of user stories. Each product owner leads their own team. Adding more teams adds more product owners, but there is still one project manager and one chief product owner deciding priorities across all the teams.

blocks.text: More teams means more product owners, not more project managers. Priorities across teams belong to the CPO.

explain.body: The organization practice defines and establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities. In agile it adds roles such as the CPO, agile coach, team coach and product owner.

test.q: Which practice answers the question 'who is accountable and responsible for what'?
test.why: The organization practice establishes the structure of accountability and responsibilities (7.1).

whyNot.0: Plans define what is to be produced and the means, with estimates of when and how much.
whyNot.1: The business case practice judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable.
whyNot.3: Progress monitors and compares actual achievements against plans.

explain.body: The PM directs the PO. The PO directs the delivery team members. Coaches and support roles advise but do not hold that authority.

test.q: The product owner role is described as a version of which PRINCE2 role?
test.why: The product owner is a version of the team manager role (Figure 7.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: User representation across the project sits with the CPO, not the PO.
whyNot.1: Project assurance monitors adherence to principles and practices independently.
whyNot.2: Change authority is delegated authority to decide on requests for change.

explain.body: One project manager, possibly several product owners, a CPO prioritizing across teams, team coaches working with one or two teams, and every team with the same make-up.

test.q: How many project managers does a PRINCE2 Agile project with five delivery teams have?
test.why: There is one project manager however many delivery teams there are (Figure 7.2).

whyNot.1: Each team may have its own product owner, but not its own project manager.
whyNot.2: Releases are timeboxes within stages; they do not get their own project manager.
whyNot.3: The same project manager runs every stage on behalf of the board.

explain.body: The PM is a servant leader linking governance and teams, and the PO is a servant leader at team level. Teams self-manage within agreed tolerances, and the board governs by exception.

test.q: Which leadership style does PRINCE2 Agile expect from the project manager?
options: Directive, assigning tasks to each developer
Servant leadership, linking governance and teams
Hands-off, leaving governance to the board
Technical, acting as lead developer for the team
test.why: The PM acts as a servant leader, facilitating collaboration between governance and teams (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Team members are led by the PO and self-manage their tasks; the PM does not assign them.
whyNot.2: The PM runs the project day to day on the board's behalf, so is not hands-off.
whyNot.3: Building products is the developers' role, not the PM's.
